1. Model consistently overestimates prices in the early part of the forecast horizon, especially after recent spikes — reduce initial forecast values by 2–5% for the first 5–7 days.

2. Model underestimates prices during prolonged downward trends — increase forecast by 3–7% in the middle of the horizon if recent history shows sustained decline.

3. Model exhibits mean reversion bias — if true outcome shows strong reversal from high to low or vice versa, adjust forecast to align with recent 7–14 day moving average.

4. Overshoot after sharp price spikes — if forecast exceeds true outcome by >10% within 3–5 days after a spike, reduce forecast by 5–15% for the next 5–10 days.

5. Model fails to capture short-term volatility — if true outcome shows rapid swings (±5%+ in 3–5 days), increase forecast variance by 10–20% in the corresponding window.

6. Horizon-specific bias — forecasts for 30-day horizon often lag true outcome by 2–4 days — adjust forecast to align with 28–30 day true outcome if available.

7. Model overreacts to recent high prices — if last 5 days are above 75, reduce forecast by 5–10% for next 7 days unless confirmed by macro indicators.

8. Model underestimates low-price periods — if true outcome shows sustained low prices (e.g., <65 for 5+ days), increase forecast by 3–8% for next 5–10 days to avoid underestimation.

9. Model exhibits “tail risk” bias — if true outcome shows sudden drop after forecast peak, reduce forecast by 10–20% for next 3–5 days to avoid overconfidence in peak.

10. Model ignores seasonal or calendar effects — if true outcome deviates from historical seasonal pattern (e.g., Q4 low), adjust forecast to align with prior 3–6 month average.
